utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. Today we are Tuesday, the 4th of March, 2008. I'd like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, Mr. Seselj, as well as all the other people assisting us. We are running a little bit late this afternoon for the simple reason that the previous hearing could not end at the expected time, so I have asked to go on for a little bit longer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, instead of starting at a quarter to 3.00, we would start at 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall hear a witness today but I would like to address the issue of tomorrow's witness, Witness number 21. I shall not give his name because he has been granted protective measures. Mr. Mundis, how do we stand to date? We have had nothing in writing, no document. I would like to mention to you that I had told Madam Dahl that I had asked to get, as was the case in the previous cases which I presided over, Hadzihasanovic and Prlic, I had asked Mrs. Dahl to give me the binders on a witness-by-witness basis, which means that I have no binder whatsoever concerning Witness 21. So I don't know why that is the case. I don't know why this hasn't been done. Therefore, at three minutes past 3.00 and 53 seconds, I would like to state that I have no document whatsoever concerning Witness 21. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. We do have those binders here with us in the courtroom, and I would ask that the usher assist in distributing them at this point in time. We are in the process of getting the consolidated 92 ter statement ERN'd, and as soon as that is available that will also be distributed along with the exhibits for that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mundis. You were saying that you have prepared a written statement, a consolidated statement, a 92 ter written statement. Now, if this witness is coming to testify tomorrow, the accused will only have this statement in his own language a few hours before the witness's testimony. I think that we face a problem here. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I have again the unERN'd version of that statement signed by the witness in B/C/S, and we are prepared to give the unERN'd version of that statement to the accused right now, Mr. President. I should also indicate that while the witness is scheduled to begin his testimony tomorrow that may or may not be the case depending upon how long it takes with the witness who is scheduled to begin testifying today. So it's possible that this witness, the 92 ter witness, will not actually commence until Thursday, but we of course will move as expeditiously as possible with the next witness, but of course it's entirely possible, if not likely that the 92 ter witness will not start tomorrow, or at the very least the cross-examination would not start until Thursday of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, I shall give you the floor. I am discovering this at the same time as you are. As far as Witness 21 is concerned, we have now the documents that have been prepared by the Prosecution. We have five exhibits which are undisputed. These are well-known lists, a few photographs. So in a few seconds, you are able to review the content of these documents. However, you do not have and I don't have the written statement. As far as you are concerned, notwithstanding the fact that you are against 92 ter statements, that is another issue, do you feel that having the statement in writing during the day, does this in any way prejudice your rights?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, evidently the OTP is now abusing the decision handed down by the Trial Chamber permitting them to bring three witnesses under Rule 92 ter. This Witness VS-021 has given several statements to date and testified in several cases. Why does the OTP need now to produce a consolidated statement by that witness? Because then that statement can be introduced directly onto the record. I can stand on my head in the courtroom, but I cannot change anything in that statement. If that is the decision you have reached, then act on it, but I abide by my decision to ignore that witness tomorrow completely. I will not raise any procedural objections. I will not listen to his abbreviated examination-in-chief introduced by the OTP along with a 92 ter statement. You have approved this because of the precedent in other cases, but you know that this happened because the Defence teams were inadequate. Had a Defence team risen to its feet and said, "I will not allow this. I will leave the courtroom," it wouldn't have happened. The lawyers here have all been bought. They don't want to lose their lucrative fees, so you can pour boiling water on them in this courtroom, if you like, and then cold ice water alternately and they will not object. You can introduce everything under Rule 92 ter and finish this trial in a few days. I will not say anything. I will sit here quietly in the dock. I guarantee that. You have seen here when several witnesses were examined, we had two, Stoparic, and a protected witness. You saw for yourselves that the witness or both witnesses said that they did not say what was contained in the statement, that they couldn't concentrate when the statement was being read out to them, that the statement was given to them for their signature in English, and the witness who is supposed to come here said that on another occasion, testifying in another case. So these are all forgeries, these statements. Any such statement -- secondly, any such statement to be admitted into evidence has to be taken according to the model used to take statements out of court. It can be valid only if I was able to cross-examine the witness when the statement was being taken, not at a later date, not subsequently. There are two things I will never accept: Introducing rules under 92 ter and quater, and I will not accept any testimony by videolink. You are right that this is provided for in the Rules. You are now applying the Rules retroactively to my case, and you may be right. You may have the right to do that. But the principle of oral testimony and the principle of direct testimony pre-date both the Statute and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this court. The principle of viva voce testimony can only be violated if we are speaking of someone who is seriously ill, seriously disabled, had his speech apparatus damaged and then that kind of person can sit here in the courtroom and write his responses. That's the only time when this principle can be laid aside. How do I know who is sitting there on the other side of the TV screen? The witness has to be brought here into the courtroom. You can do what you like but I have told you my opinion. In my view, the major problem is not the fact that the OTP has not prepared the material in time. A bigger problem is the willingness of the Chamber to accept 92 ter testimony. You have said that you will allow such witnesses only when someone turns up testifying to a same issue so that the testimony is cumulative. It's the same issue mentioned by other witnesses. But now you're introducing three witnesses under Rule 92 ter and not one of them has testified about that particular crime base. There's another issue I want to raise now that I have the floor although it's difficult for me to speak today. The witness who is supposed to come today has been announced as a crime base witness. The first sentence in the pro memoria, in the memo for that witness says that the witness will testify to the crime base in Western Slavonia. And you have handed down a decision more than once, as did your predecessors, that this crime base will not be brought up in the courtroom, and I am amazed at all the changes that are taking place here. I can't follow things properly. I don't know what's going on. Are we having testimony here about the crime base in Western Slavonia or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several things. First of all, I have realised something, Mr. Seselj. Last week you told me that you had a bout of asthma, and now you've just said, if I've understood correctly, that you've had a few problems. Can you confirm that you're suffering from asthma right now or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is the season of the year when I have this problem, and a virus is also going around. I've noticed that with the other people in detention in Scheveningen and it's making my asthma a bit more serious, but I am not in so bad a condition that I cannot follow the trial or sit here. It will pass in a few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me get back to your bout of asthma, because this was a topic which you addressed when I was a Judge during the pre-trial stage, and you mentioned the atmosphere in your cell, and at the time we had expeditiously sent experts to your cell to see whether the air in your cell was conducive to asthma in any way, but as this had been settled at the time, are you currently taking any medicines such as Ventolin? Because if you have a sudden attack of asthma, you can then use your spray and contain the asthma.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm constantly taking medicaments for asthma. I have them in my pocket so I don't foresee any special problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So good. I feel very reassured by this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I just want to make sure that I understand your standpoint in relation to the application of Rule 92 ter correctly, because what I don't understand is what difference it makes to you whether a witness comes here and testifies viva voce under Rule 65 ter and during his testimony a statement that he has given and signed is introduced into evidence. That is one situation. And the other situation is exactly the same thing happening except that the statement is admitted through 92 ter. The witness is here. He's open to you to cross-examination, he's open to questions from the Court in both cases. So what damage is done to your case by introducing a witness statement under Rule 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle -- or, rather, the principle of viva voce testimony means that the witness must be able to tell his story in the courtroom in front of us all. We saw from the Stoparic example and the example of VS-004 that their stories deviated significantly from what was in their statement, especially Witness Stoparic said he never said those things. Do you remember that in the statement it said that I greeted the people at the rally with the Hitler salute, and the witness denied it all when he came to the courtroom. In a number of cases you can see that witnesses said their statements contained things they hadn't said. At least 40 witnesses in the Milosevic case said that what was in the statement were not their words. Now, look here. What sort of statement is it by the witness when it's written down by someone from the OTP, when they sign it in English, and when after many hours of interviews somebody else prepares the statement? You heard what Stoparic said. He wanted it to be over as soon as possible. He just wanted to sign and be done with it. So you're accepting in advance to have something on the record that was written by the OTP. What the OTP writes down is simply an addendum to the indictment. It's not evidence. Otherwise, the indictment itself would be evidence, because the OTP compiled the indictment based on many statements. But an indictment cannot be evidence. Nothing that the OTP writes can be evidence, and those statements were written by the OTP. Had that statement been taken by rules governing depositions, that would be another matter. We can have a witness who is unavailable, who is serving time in another prison, it's too dangerous to bring him here. Then somebody from the Chamber, from the Registry, from the OTP, and from the Defence has to go and interview the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I can hear what you're saying but you're not answering my question. In both instances the witness will be here to tell his story and in both instances you will be able to cross-examine him. So what difference does it make whether he comes under one or the other form?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The difference is in that case it's much easier to manipulate the witness, and I delivered to you two statements by legal advisors of Slobodan Milosevic who suspected in the case of a number of witnesses that somebody was dictating to them through their headsets in the courtroom what sort of answers they should give. That is very easy to do technically. That's one of the reasons. Secondly, a witness can give brief replies, yes and no, that simply neutralise my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, my fellow Judge has clearly indicated with his questions that according to him and according to me, and I believe my fellow Judge to my left also agrees with me, this procedure does not prejudice you in any way, but you seem to be concerned about Witness 21. I'm not going to give his name, but let me remind you that the Prosecution had filed a motion, a confidential motion, an ex parte motion on the 22nd of October, 2007, and stipulated or asked for the admission of the transcripts during witness testimony during other trials. The Trial Chamber handed down its decision on the 22nd of February, 2008, and we dismissed this request and indicated to the Prosecution that it could, if need be, seize us of a motion on the basis of a new statement provided for these witness under the condition that this motion be introduced 14 days before the witness's testimony in question and before having the translation in your language. So the 14-day deadline has not, in this particular instance, been abided by. So this is why this will be discussed by the Trial Chamber a little later today. As far as I'm concerned, I'm against the 92 ter procedure in the case of this witness, because our decision has not been abided by. We have taken this decision to protect your rights, so that transcripts concerning these witnesses are not admitted when the questions that might arise might have no direct connection with you and may have nothing to do with the presentation of your case. This is why we had asked the Prosecution to prepare a new written statement, and it is with this in mind that the Prosecution did prepare a new written statement, but they did this in somewhat of a hurry and called this witness to testify rather quickly without enabling you to look into the statement in detail. So this is what the problem is all about. Now, in what way would you be prejudiced? I think the whole question hinges on this. If we have a written statement -- let's take any witness. If we have a written statement, the witness then explains what he -- his training was, what kind of studies he undertook, what unit he was part of, and then what does the Prosecution do when it's a viva voce witness? The Prosecution then has the written statement before him or her and then puts questions in line or in the same order as the written statement. For instance: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what did you do between 1990 and 1991? And the witness will say, "1990 and 1991, I did such-and-such," and the witness will repeat what is already contained in the written statement, and this is how this will unfold. Rather than wasting time at this game and the Prosecution puts question to the witness and the witness repeats what has already been said, we can gain time by admitting the written statement. But the accused has the written statement before him, and the accused can in that case look at those paragraphs which are relevant to his case. And at the time of the cross-examination, you can then put your questions. You're not prejudiced in any way. You would be prejudiced if the Prosecutor were to ask him to say what is in the statement. If the lawyer does not put the right question, which is not your case because you are representing yourself in this case, the accused -- or if the accused would not be putting the right questions, then there could be prejudice, but this is not the case because you are defending your own case. So you are not going to overlook anything that's contained in the written statement. And in addition, you have a Trial Chamber before you that puts a lot of questions. So you can imagine that if in the written statement there is something that is essential, the Bench will put questions to the witness. They will not overlook this important point. This is why it is so difficult for us to understand why you are opposed to this. You have explained this to us many a time, and you have said, "If it's like that, I shall not put any questions." I find that rather difficult to understand. If you felt prejudiced, I would agree with you and support you, but in this case I really don't see in what way you would be prejudiced. If there were a prejudice, tell us in what way you would be prejudiced, because you can, during cross-examination, ask all the questions you wish to put to the witness, and you can then highlight the fact that the written statement is not in line or does not match the truth, because you are the one putting the questions. It's not a counsel who is putting the questions for you. So you also have a Trial Chamber that scrutinises all of this. So in what way would you be prejudiced? If you are able to convince us that you are being prejudiced, we shall listen to you; but today as things stand, the three Judges that make up the Bench do not see in what way you are prejudiced. I'll give the floor back to you, and tell us and let he is know why you believe you are prejudiced. If you are able to convince us, then we will revert to viva voce witnesses, but we are not convinced that you are prejudiced. We'll give the floor back to you, Mr. Seselj. Explain to us in what way you feel you're prejudiced.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, a written statement by the witness cannot be admitted either in continental or Anglo Saxon law. This is something new, invented by this international Tribunal. Secondly, it violates the principle of orality, viva voce of testimony. Also, it violates the principle of directness. As soon as a traditional principle of law is violated, this prejudices my case. Secondly, instead of viva voce testimony, a statement is admitted into the file, into the record directly. The statement was written by the OTP. It was only signed by the witness who confirms it is his here in the courtroom but sometimes the witness does that without even reading the statement. So the OTP is producing evidence directly. As you have seen, the OTP is also introducing expert reports, writing expert reports directly. Why doesn't the OTP then write the judgement also. I want to hear the story told by the witness directly. Not a single witness is able to tell the story in the words written for him by the OTP, not a single one, unless someone learns it off by heart. You know, there's a title in Islam. A person is called an Hafiz if they can memorise the entire Koran, and among the witnesses there may be such people with such memories, but average people are unable to memorise things in this way. And it's simply not the same story. It's simply not the same testimony. The OTP is distilling the witness testimony and shaping it in order for it to support the indictment in the best possible way for them, and this is creative work by the OTP. And in that creative work, the OTP gives itself the freedom and the liberty to invent things that the witness never said such as my alleged Nazi salute. The witness said he never heard -- he never said that. I can, of course, cross-examine, but my cross-examination is much more effective if I can compare the statement given to me by the OTP and the story told by the witness in the courtroom, and I can then tell the witness, I can put it to him, "Well, you said so-and-so in the statement and now you're saying something else." And then the witness can say, "Well, when I signed the statement I wasn't concentrating, I overlooked this and so on and so forth." But once the statement is admitted into evidence I no longer have the possibility of doing this. As you know, every witness is proofed. He's thoroughly prepared for his testimony, and in this case it's much easier to proof the witness and prepare him, such as when they tell their experts to give expansive answers, to waste my time, to avoid answering certain questions directly and so on and so forth. Now they can teach the witness to say, "I don't remember. I --" and so on and so forth and it's all admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you are mistaken in a number of ways. With all due respect, I'm going to point out these mistakes. You say that in civil law countries, written statement are not admitted as evidence. That's not true. In your country, in Denmark, in Italy, in France, an investigation is conducted by the police, a written statement taken by the police, and then this statement is part and parcel of the case file. The exact same thing happens here. Written statements are taken by investigators. Most of the time they are former policemen, and they take the statements of witnesses. The only difference is that in your country there is an investigative judge and not here. But here we have an adversarial system, a common law system, and thus you are in a position to cross-examine your witnesses. Second mistake I'd like to point out. You say that the statement is admitted. No. The statement is only admitted at the very end, and it's only admitted if it's -- if it looks credible and if no mistakes have appeared during the cross-examination. Let me give an example. This Nazi salute, in the written statement it is said -- let's assume it said that Mr. X made a Nazi salute, and then you can ask the witness during cross-examination, "You said in your written statement that you saw someone make a Nazi salute," and then the witness could say, "No. I've never said any such thing." The conclusion then would be that the investigator put these words in the witness's mouth, and therefore the written statement has much less weight. During the cross-examination, you will be able to review the written statement point by point. Only at the end of the cross-examination will we decide to admit this written statement or not. If you completely destroyed the written statement during your cross-examination, then the written statement will not be admitted. On the other hand, if you highlight a number of points in the written statements that are not credible, then the Chamber will not take these points into account. Because you have to remember that when we render our judgement at the end, we'll need to give reasons for every one of our conclusions of our holdings, and our judgement will be based on all evidence, on written statements, on testimonies, on the answers given to -- by the witness to everyone. Therefore, there can be no prejudice, you see. You tell us that the written statement in English comes from the OTP. Yes, you're right. A member of the OTP staff has drafted that statement, but theoretically the statement reflects what the witness has said. And the OTP's not going to go around making false statements, because if that appeared to be the case, the Trial Chamber could call the investigator and put questions to him. So you see, your rights are guaranteed. You've decided to adopt a negative attitude and to reject the principle of these written statements. You say that they're not credible. They're false. You say that witnesses are manipulated and at one point you said that witnesses, they are told what to answer in their earphones. Believe me we can check all that and when we listen to a witness, me and my fellow Judges, if we identify any problem, any failings in the testimony, we will put the right questions to the witness. Our mission is to establish the truth, the truth in the interests of justice, not in your interest, not in the interests of the Prosecutor. The Judges have the role to play when the witness is here. They do not only rely on the written statement. Fine. I believe that we've covered everything. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm just going to focus on the first part of what you've said. You're quite right when you say that both in my country and your country and some other countries as well a statement given at the police station is part and parcel of the case files, but only if we're talking about suspects. They are suspects in front of the police, and then the police tells them that they can take a lawyer and have the assistance of a lawyer or give that right up. So the statement can be introduced into the files straight away. However, a witness statement does not go into the files straight away. The witness must testify in the courtroom orally on -- based on the principle of oral testimony and direct testimony. And I'll present another problem now. For one of these three witnesses that will come under 92 ter, the OTP provided me with documents saying that the Croatian intelligence service had interrogated him, that he went through a briefing and was told how he should behave here, and it's a public secret that this is what the Muslim secret service does, too, when we're dealing with Muslims, Muslims witnesses. We have a series of witnesses. The AID of the time that -- the A-I-D, AID prepared witnesses. So witnesses are prepared and proofed when it comes to the opposite side. They are prepared by their national police services, and here in the Tribunal they are prepared by the OTP. And then a statement is taken so that he is deprived the right of telling his story in the courtroom. Now, if a witness is going to tell the truth, his story will basically be the same at all times. And if the witness lied on several occasions and if they are lengthy lies, then he's not capable of repeating all those lies in court. And you saw this with Witness Stoparic. His lies were reduced to the question of Vojvodina. He derided all the other true lies from his statement. The only thing that remained was what Natasa Kandic told him what was the key issue and what he should insist upon. So the same will happen with these other witnesses. So witnesses are prepared in twofold fashion, and there's absolutely no doubt that this was done in many other trials as well. And the Defence does not have any means of counteracting this, standing up to it. I have only one way of doing that and that is to refuse to take part in presenting witnesses in this way. That's the only road open to me. And I'm not going to disrupt the proceedings here by any of my gestures. I'm going to sit here quietly. I won't say a single word, and I'll just watch and see what's going on. I'm not going to look at the documents. I could even take off my headset and not listen to anything being said in court. So you won't have any problems with me, but I am not going to participate in any of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Mundis, you wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd just like to respond very quickly to two or three issues that arose and then I do have two other issues that I'd like to raise with the Chamber. First of all, the Prosecution categorically denies and refutes the notion that we prepare witnesses or tell witnesses what to say. I'm not going to go into that in any greater detail because quite frankly I don't think it merits a response. Let me just say a couple of things with respect to the issue of 92 ter statements and the 92 ter statement that was provided just a few moments ago. There is nothing of any significance that is new in this consolidated statement that has been prepared when carefully compared to the witness's prior statements and prior testimony. What we have done is simply taken the prior statements, taken the prior transcript testimony and consolidated and focused that material into one single statement that makes it easier for the Trial Chamber to follow and makes it easier for Dr. Seselj to prepare his cross-examination. The statement, as will be the case with all the proposed 92 ter statements, are signed by the witness in B/C/S. So the entire issue of a statement in English that's signed by the witness is moot. The 92 ter statements will be signed in the language of the witness. I'd like to also respond to a couple of points concerning what Dr. Seselj said with respect to cross-examining earlier witnesses and those witnesses' statements with respect to their written statements or what they testified in court about concerning their written statements. Again, that's not an issue with respect to 92 ter statements for the simple reason that the statement is, again, in the language of the witness. So we're not talking about a situation where a witness is being questioned about statements that were signed in a language that the witness does not understand. With respect to the timing issue, we're certainly sensitive to than point, but I would like to stress, and I believe the Chamber's well aware of this, that we have had problems lining up witnesses in this case, witnesses who at the last moment are refusing to travel to The Hague and testifying, and our choice is then to re-jiggle the schedule, which combined with time pressures have led us to choose the course set forth in the Rules and jurisprudence under Rule 92 ter in order for us to get all of the evidence before the Trial Chamber in the amount of time allocated, taking into consideration a number of factors such as the refusal of some witnesses to travel to The Hague and testify. And that's really all I have to say, Your Honours, about Rule 92 ter and the application thereof in this case. But I do have two other points if I may at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Before I let you cover these two points, when you were speaking I was looking at the written statement of Witness 21. There are 67 paragraphs in that statement. It took only a few seconds for me to realise that in these 67 paragraphs no mention is made of Mr. Seselj or of the volunteers. This is a factual statement about what took place in Vukovar, bombing the hospital, detainees, and so on and so forth. Mr. Seselj, there's nothing in this statement that might prejudice you, nothing at all in those 67 paragraphs. By tomorrow, by Thursday, please take the time to read this statement, the statement of this witness. You will realise that there's no ground to attack the proceedings based on this witness. This could even have been a 92 bis witness. Please read the statement. It took me only a few seconds to glance through it. And believe me, most of the Tribunal's Judges would admit it as a 92 bis witness because there's nothing related to your actions or to your behaviour. It's a purely factual statement. I don't see why you could not cross-examine the witness on events that are quite well-known and that apparently you've never chosen to -- chosen to challenge. I don't see where problem is. If it was a much more significant witness, the Chamber would refuse that procedure and would require the witness to be heard viva voce, but I'm telling you, as far as you're concerned, there is no prejudice here regarding this witness. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if your main problem is time, time concerns, and I assume that that is the case, then the Prosecution is the main culprit for not saving a lot of time, because it's been almost five years since I have requested that I meet with the OTP, with my legal advisors, and the investigators, and to look at the facts not to challenge them or to challenge them. I am not challenging that a crime took place at Ovcara. So these are things that could have been resolved preliminarily and we would have saved a lot of time in that way and then we could look and see who was to blame for the crimes where they are undisputed. But there are a series of other questions which could have been resolved in those five years, preliminary five years, but the OTP avoided doing that because the OTP wanted to select my legal advisors, who could and couldn't be a legal advisor. They wanted to impose counsel on me and then to get through all this material with that counsel and that's not my fault. We have too many witnesses on the witness list; 105 witnesses testifying about all and sundry. There is not even a third that could be called relevant witnesses as far as this trial is concerned. So it's ludicrous to call all those witnesses. Next, if you don't allow the OTP to prove the database and crime base, the Prosecution says the crime base is Western Slavonia, for example, to start off with. Now, I don't understand how something like that can happen and you tolerate it. Do we need three witnesses to prove that the crime in Ovcara took place? I think one would be sufficient. And then when you see that I do not deny the crime itself, and then we have forensic experts and two Croatian experts coming in afterwards who dealt with the exhumation of the bodies, not to mention the names, I think they're protected too, then there will be a Serbian witness who is not protected. He was a one-time minister of defence and he's a pathologist himself. So why are they doing all that? One witness would be sufficient for the database as far as the crime at Ovcara is concern. You would be able to see that I'm not challenging that a crime actually took place and that 200 prisoners of war were executed. I'm not contesting that or something that has not got anything to do with his testimony then you wouldn't need the other two witnesses at all because you have proof and evidence on the basis of the transcript, that I'm not challenging or contesting the fact that a crime took place. So why this irrational conduct on the part of the OTP? Now for principled reasons when principles are being violated, I'm always prejudiced and as soon as legal principles are being violated, I consider that that is prejudice against me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you came on the case in the middle. You may not be aware that during the pre-trial stage Mr. Seselj suggested that he meet the OTP. He said that very officially, and at the time I drew Ms. Dahl's attention on the fact, saying that Mr. Seselj was ready to meet with you. It did not happen. There was some obstruction, I don't know where, but Mr. Seselj at the time said that some crimes could not be denied. Of course he denies that these crimes can be -- can -- that he may be made responsible for these crimes, but that's something else. The OTP did not respond to the offer of a meeting with Mr. Seselj. We are talking about Ovcara, but there may be other cases, other crimes that were committed. Why do we have five, ten witnesses who will come here to establish this crime, and the witnesses won't even tell us who did what. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And an additional observation before Mr. Mundis, if I may. In 2003, that was the offer I made to the OTP. Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff accepted. However, she did not want to accept my legal advisors to be present. You'll be able to find that in the documents. I can provide you with the documents if you can't find them in the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I believe actually there's -- there's a couple of issues that are -- that are related here in what we've just heard. My understanding is that earlier, what was being proposed was a limited number of agreed facts, not necessarily more overarching crime base such as Ovcara, which we've heard now being indicated by Dr. Seselj that he's not contesting that crimes actually occurred there. I am going to undertake a review of what was previously said, and my understanding as well is that a letter did go from Mrs. Dahl to the accused on this issue as well. I don't have that in front of me. I don't, therefore, want to go into the specifics of that, but I will state two points, two additional points on this matter. First of all, sometimes it's necessary, even though specific events or specific crime or crime bases are admitted to, sometimes it's still necessary to call witnesses in order to identify the actual perpetrator or in order to link those crimes which even though the fact that the crime was committed has been admitted or agreed to, to link that to the accused. So the fact that -- that crimes have been agreed to or admitted to does not always mean that there is no need to call the witnesses with respect to those crimes. That's point one. Point two is, again, once we've undertaken a review to determine exactly what was previously said on this point and what the issues are, I can assure the Trial Chamber that if it would be productive for the Prosecution to meet with Dr. Seselj and his team, we will do so. And if in the very near future it becomes perhaps productive or necessary for us to ask the Chamber not to sit for a certain number of days so that we can do that, I can guarantee you that we will in fact take such steps. At this point I don't want to take that any further until I've been able to review the prior transcripts as well as any prior correspondence relating to this point, but -- but if we believe it would be productive to sit down and meet to discuss a number of issues, whether it's agreed facts or specific crimes and the admission of specific crimes or the fact that they actually occurred, we will do so. I want to make that absolutely clear that we have no intention of bringing in a string of witnesses or victims to testify about events that the accused is not contesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You wanted to add two more things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The first issue, Mr. President, concerns submission of the accused number 375. This concerns -- or this was a notice that the accused filed indicating that he had returned a DVD containing Annex B2 to the Prosecution motion for leave to add exhibits to its 65 ter list filed on 24 December 2007. I would note for the record that on 11 January 2008, the Prosecution filed a motion to withdraw the motion that had been filed on 24 December 2007. Therefore, in our respectful view, the accused's submission number 375 is moot and requires no further action, at least from the Prosecution. So that if the Chamber were amenable or felt it necessary to render a decision on submission 375, you are certainly free to do so because there will be no further submissions from the Prosecution since that submission of the accused relates to a motion which we have withdrawn, and I want to put that on the record to close that issue as far as we're concerned. The second issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The second issue, Mr. President and Your Honours, concerns a topic that has arisen several times in the last few weeks. This concerns the hard copy disclosure of a large volume of material. In the last two weeks the accused has raised the issue of documents that he had rejected when they were disclosed to him in an electronic format on 30 September 2004. This was raised at the hearing on 21 February 2008, commencing at page 3990 of the transcript, and it arose again on 25 February 2008. This concerns the more than 200.000 pages of material that the Trial Chamber is aware of and which, again, has been raised a number of times. As is clear from the transcript of the hearing held on 4 July 2007, the accused fully appreciates that the material in question has been identified based on a number of searches for so-called perpetrator organisations. The accused's position has been that since this material is potentially exculpatory, he has requested the Prosecution to provide this material to him in hard copy. He has also indicated that he does not trust the Prosecution to review this material, and in this respect, I draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the transcript at pages 1234, 1300, and pages 1339 through 1340. This position was repeated by Dr. Seselj at the Pre-Trial Conference on 23 October 2007, at transcript pages 1645 through 1647. And as I understood what Dr. Seselj said at the hearing on 21 February 2008, he still maintains that he would like this material in hard copy. The Prosecution agrees to the accused's request and will initiate the reproduction of this material in hard copy as soon as possible. I am not standing here today in a position to give a date certain when that material might be delivered to the accused. I do expect, however, that we will be in a position to begin disclosing this material in approximately three weeks and that this disclosure will be complete in approximately six weeks. We will put this material into binders in ERN order, and we will provide Dr. Seselj with an index of this material. It's my understanding that the accused wishes to review all of this material himself as he believes it contains material that falls within Rule 68(i), and he does not trust the Prosecution to review it. While it is obviously up to him to decide how he will review the material, we will, as I've indicated provide him with a number of indices specifying in which documents the various perpetrator groups are mentioned and in which documents the name of crime base locations can be found. Before the Prosecution begins the reproduction of this material, however, I want to be certain that the scope of this hard copy disclosure is fully understood. The total volume of this material amounts to 306.000 pages. We will put this in binders. We are talking somewhere in the neighbourhood of 620 large lever-arch binders, which will fill approximately 12 to 15 standard-sized metal cabinets. I will indicate that all of this material is also available in EDS, the electronic disclosure suite. I understand the accused refuses to use that tool, but it is all available in EDS, and he does have access to it. At this point, Your Honours, what I am simply asking is for a determination from the accused himself in light of what I have just told Your Honours and the accused to confirm that he in fact wants this material in hard copy rather than in an electronic format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Mr. Seselj, just -- I would like just to go back a little bit in time. During a pre-trial hearing, Mr. Seselj, on the 30th of September, 2004, indicated that there were 207.000 pages that came under Rule 68, and at the time, let me remind you of all of this, this is extremely important. Rule 68 had been amended on the 28th of July, 2004. I attended the session during which this Rule was amended. And a few days later, less than a month later, your colleague who preceded you sent this letter off stating that there were 207.000 pages. From what I understood when your colleague sent this letter off, she knew that Mr. Seselj had a standby counsel at the time, and she had said to herself, well, the standby counsel will conduct the research in the electronic system, and she hadn't asked herself the question that, i.e., that the accused might one of these days represent himself and defend himself and, therefore, these documents had to be provided to him in his own language and in hard copy. This is how things started off to begin with. This started to begin with -- Rule 68 had been amended. Paragraph (i) and (ii) mentions disclosure electronically, and the first paragraph does not mention this. And when an accused is representing himself, when an accused does not wish to use the computer system, he then has to resort to hard copies. It took me a while to identify the problem and now that I'm able to put my finger on it, I know actually what happened. I'm sure you have understood what the problem is all about. This is why you have now formally told us that you would send all these documents to Mr. Seselj, 300.000 pages approximately, and this amounts to 620 large binders that could be put into 10 to 12 filing cabinets. Mr. Seselj, are you able in three weeks' time, because the Prosecution has just told us that he needs approximately three weeks, are you able in your cell or in the next door cell receive 600 binders? This is in line with your request. You asked for this. So the Prosecution is meeting request. Are you able on your own to use these 600 binders purposefully and read 300.000 pages?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've been fighting for this for five years now. I can read it on my own, and my associates will help on this. 300.000 pages, well, you know, if this was all serious material, then it couldn't be read in a lifetime, but you can just leaf through it. You leaf through it, and you leaf through it, and when you come across something interesting you stop, and then there's diagonal reading. There are various systems that can be used. I am prepared to accept this. Let the authorities in the detention unit give me place to store this. They've given me another cell. Let them give me two more. There are plenty of empty cells in the detention unit. But something what is much more important for me is something else here. You will recall last year we had frequent Status Conferences, at least once a month, and at each and every one of those we spoke about the disclosure of material under Rule 68(i), and Madam Christine Dahl kept avoiding this and rejecting this. Now Mr. Mundis says that in six weeks they're ready to do all of that and that they even have a hundred thousand pages more than I asked for. I asked for 207.000 pages and they have 300.000 pages, and that is a job that can be done in six weeks. Imagine if it had been down in March or April or June or July of last year. I would have been in a much better position as regards the preparation of my defence and yet I had to wait for half the trial to be over or at least half the Prosecution case to be over before I get this. That's another problem that has now been revealed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not halfway. We have just started. We're not halfway. We have heard a few witnesses. So, Mr. Mundis, Mr. Seselj agrees to receive all the 620 binders which will fill 10 to 12 filing cabinets. He is waiting for these documents now, so it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And during the next break I will ensure that this project gets underway in earnest. I can tell from the look of the registrar's face that he's looking forward to receiving that material as well, so we will begin that process. I would expect it will take between three -- three weeks for the material to begin arriving and six weeks for the entire project to be complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At least this is a good piece of news. So I don't know whether it's a good piece of news for whom, but for the rights of the accused, I think that's pretty obvious. So -- maybe not for the registrar, who seems to be overwhelmed. Now, let's bring in the witness. So the witness has not been granted any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I want to just check that you are able to hear the translation of what I'm saying in your own language. If you are able to hear me, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, can you give me your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Mladen Kulic. I was born on the 1st of October, 1946.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have an occupation currently, and if you do, please tell us which one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm not employed at present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you already testified in any trial? If so, which one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified in 2002 in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. According to my research work, in 2002 you were granted protective measures. Today you have not been granted protective measures for your testimony. For what reason have you decided to testify publicly, in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, circumstances have changed somewhat so that is why my estimate is that I can testify like this now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the representative from the Prosecution some very brief information I would like to convey to you. You, sir, will have to answer questions that will be put to you by the representative of the Prosecution whom we have granted two hours to put questions to you. The representative of the Prosecution will show you a number of documents in support of his questions. After this phase, Mr. Seselj who is seated to your left will also put questions to you as part of the cross-examination. The three Judges that make up the Bench can also at any time put questions to you on the basis of some of the documents or on the basis of some of the answers you provide to one or other party. Generally, we have a break every hour and a half so that you can have a 20-minute break. If you don't understand the meaning of the question, please do not hesitate to ask the person who has put the question to you to rephrase it. If at some point in time you don't feel well, don't hesitate to raise your hand and let us know so that we can adjourn the hearing instantly and make sure that you have an appropriate rest. If you feel at some point in time you would like to address the Chamber, do not hesitate to put any question which you may deem useful, because we shall be prepared to listen to you. This is what I wanted to convey to you, and I shall now give the floor to the representative of the Prosecution, who is going to start his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, before I start -- before I start to put questions to the witness, let me please correct some information. You said at the beginning that this witness has not been granted protective measures. This is not completely correct. He has been granted protective measures with a decision on 30th of August, 2007, paragraphs (ii) and (vi). He has got pseudonym and face distortion. But during proofing the witness told me that he does not need these protective measures any longer. This is the reason why he wants to testify now in open session without any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I agree with you. When I said that there were no protective measures, as of today, that is what I meant. Before today, of course, there were protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, could you please tell us what is your nationality, and what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I am a national of the Republic of Croatia, and by nationality I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Are you married and do you have children?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I am not married, but I do have children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please describe us your professional background. What is your -- what was your professional education?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I graduated in economy. I'm an economist. I graduated in 1978 at Osijek University, the Faculty of Economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Please tell us, when did you finish your studies?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I -- as I said, I graduated in 1978. I was working also before that. I got another degree at the same university in '74, which was an intermediate degree. I studied economics at Novi Sad and at Subotica, but because of financial circumstances and because at that faculty you could not study by degrees as you could in Osijek, I first did my military service, and then I continued my studies. That's the history of my university studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Please tell us what did you do between 1969 and 1971, apart from studying?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: In 1969, because of my financial situation, because I couldn't afford to continue my studies in the regular way, I got a job in Podravska Slatina in the Municipal Assembly, as it was then called, and then I continued studying along with my work. I first got the intermediate degree and then I got the actual bachelor's degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What was your task when you worked between 1969 and 1971?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I was employed in the Municipal Assembly in a newly established body. Its precise name at the time was the Staff of the Territorial Defence. It's an organ which by a decision of the Podravska Slatina Municipal Assembly was established in 1968 and I was the first person employed on organising work there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When you studied to work in the profession you studied or in the job you studied, can you please tell us where did you start your work, at what company?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: When I completed the first degree of the Faculty of Economics in Osijek, I had to pass some extra exams in 1974, and then I paused. I took a break because I couldn't continue working and studying at the same time. So then I completed my studies in the regular way and sometime in February 1974 I took my degree, and I immediately got employment in Podravska Slatina in the industrial and agricultural complex called Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you change your work employment sometime during your professional life?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I completed that school, because there were insufficient staff in Podravska Slatina and in other companies they needed people like me, and then I went to work in Univerzal where I was in charge of the finance department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What kind of company was this?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: It was a metalworking industry. We produced curing sheds for tobacco production.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What did you do after you finished working for that company?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: In late 1996, I returned to my previous company, the industrial agricultural complex Osijek in the part dealing with fruit and vegetable processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. I refer to --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I refer to the years 1983 and not 1996. That's a too big gap.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. In 1983, I left the place of director of the Univerzal metalworking industry. In the meantime, from chief of the finance department I was promoted to the post of managing director where I stayed for one term from 1979 to 1983. After that, I went back to the Municipal Assembly of Podravska Slatina, but I went to work in what was then called the institute for social planning and statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: How would you describe your job at that time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: My job in the institute for social planning and statistics was to do with my profession. Based on my experience in the enterprises I had worked in and my financial expertise, I was an economic analyst for the Podravska Slatina municipality. After that, I also became the director of that institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Is it correct that your last position was that of a director?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1991, I was director of the institute for social planning and statistics of the Podravska Slatina municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What was -- did you finish this job and when?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of May, 1991, the government commissioner of the Republic of Croatia, Ante Simara relieved me of my duty. He dismissed me, me and many others, mostly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Who was Ante Simara?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Ante Simara was the commissioner of the government of Croatia because the executive organ of the Municipal Assembly had been disbanded. He was the president of the HDZ for the Podravska Slatina municipality, and also the president of the Podravska Slatina Crisis Staff. That was the information I had about what he was doing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have also other persons been removed from their job?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Yes. All my friends and many other Serbs were dismissed from their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Only Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: In the Municipal Assembly all the Serbs, and in other organisations there were other -- no, only Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I will now come to another issue. Have you ever been politically engaged?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you lost your job because you were a Serb. You studied at the economics faculty. At the time could you have seized a tribunal to challenge your dismissal which had obviously taken place for ethnic reasons? Was that something you could have done? Was that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ... possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why didn't you do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to explain this. On the 31st of May, 1991, when the government of Croatia appointed the commissioner of the Municipal Assembly of Podravska Slatina to take over the function of the Executive Council, Ante Simara, he took it upon himself to reorganise things, and he dismissed people, all of us, in such a way that we continued receiving salaries until the 31st of August, 1991. They said we were on standby. That's what they called it. There was no reason at that point for me to sue the State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But after the 31st of August, 1991, you weren't on the payroll any more, so you had been dismissed from then on, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, right now it's very important to explain what the circumstances were that prevailed from the 31st of May to the 31st of August. There were other problems, and the question was whether one should enter into legal proceedings when one was worried about saving one's life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time Yugoslavia was a federal republic, wasn't it? Now when someone is dismissed, you were still in Yugoslavia, so the political bodies were sometimes in the minority. HDZ -- the HDZ had taken control. Could it have not turned to the federal authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on the 31st of August, Yugoslavia existed only formally. Concerning my republic at the time, there were no communications any more. On the 31st of August, there was already a state of war. It was a situation where -- how can I explain this? There was shooting going on. People were being killed. Property was being damaged. There was no communication among the republics of the former Yugoslavia any more. And all these were circumstances which put one in a dilemma whether to try and save one's life, save your life and the life of your family. So it was no longer -- it was no longer so important to seek your employment rights when you no longer had any right to a home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answers. I'm sure we will be able to better understand things in the course of your testimony. I'll give the floor back to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, you told us that you had never been politically engaged. Can you give us the reasons for that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Well, some might challenge what I'm saying now because up to 1988 -- from 1964 to 1988, I was actually a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. From 1988, I was no longer a member. When I say I was not involved in politics, what I want to say is that I never held a post where I could carry out any special political tasks, let alone create policies and influence the situation around me. I was a member on paper, yes. I paid my dues to the party. I sometimes attended meetings when I was summoned, but I was never in the leading structures of that party, and that's why I say I was not involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please describe us the political situation in your region in 1990 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. We shall have the break now, and you can put your question again after the break. It's now time to stop and have a break. So we shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed. The Prosecutor needs to ask the last question again. Let me just tell you that at five to 6.00 we'll have a ten-minute break and then we'll resume at 5 past 6.00 until 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the last question I put to you was: Please describe us what was the political situation in 1990 and 1991 in your area.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: In 1990 as was common knowledge after the parliamentary elections in Croatia, the Croatian Democratic Party came into power, the HDZ, and at the time in the Croatia there were about 12.5 per cent Serbs who mostly voted for the Party of Democratic Change or the SDP party. They changed their name at the time. Now, with these changes in power and authority, the changes on the political scene, in fact, with the arrival of the Croatian Democratic Community, conditions changed for one and all because in the pre-election campaign itself we could see quite clearly the policy that was waged -- that was going to be waged by the Croatian Democratic Union if it came into power, the HDZ. First of all, it was a national policy, a nationalist policy, and already at the time it was recognisable as a nationalist party, and that is what it proved to be. With the changes in the constitution in 1990, the Serbs as a constituent people were wiped out. They became a minority regardless of their contribution to the creation of Croatia, and their contribution to the development of Croatia. In this way, immediately after the elections everything that was said in the pre-election campaign proved to be even worse later on, even more black for the position of the Serbs. There was no attempt at resolving the problem peacefully. The Croatian state attempted in all places where the Serbs were in the majority and Serbs who didn't agree to the terror over them to be detained, taken into custody, and so on, but I have to say that in the meantime the Serbs began to organise themselves on a national basis, too, and the Serbian Democratic Party was formed along those lines, and in some places earlier, in some places later. In my region, Podravska Slatina, the Serbian Democratic Party was formed at the beginning of 1991, for instance. And the people who had been in the SDP until then, and they were in the Municipal Assembly, for example, as delegates there, they set up their own SDP club. I'm sorry, I meant SDS club. In the political sense this didn't lead towards a dialogue, but it led to confrontation. And in the meantime, at the beginning of 1991, as you already know, incidents broke out, different incidents. And when I say that, I mean the escalation of the conflict in general, which was nationalistically coloured, that is to say a conflict between the Serbs and Croats. Let me mention that from Pakrac, 1993, which is my general area, because my place belongs to Western Slavonia as does Pakrac, then in April at Lake Plitvice, then in Borovo Selo, in May and so on and so forth, for you to be able to understand the situation, let me say that 1991 proved a year of escalation and took on the contours of war, a war conflict. And in all these places you had the presence of police forces that came into play. The group of citizens and the National Guards Corps, which was established in the meantime, launched an attack on the barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Witness. I'm sorry for interrupt you. I would like to know if there has been any tolerance between the nationalities --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. Mr. President, I don't think the Prosecution has the right to interrupt the witness. He has to allow the witness to complete his answer. He can't pick and choose what he likes and what he doesn't like, and when he doesn't like something the witness says to interrupt him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you were interrupted. Had you completed your answer or did you want to expand on your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This topic, Your Honour, is a very broad one, and I wanted briefly to paint a picture in response to what the Prosecutor asked me with respect to the atmosphere that prevailed at the time, the climate that prevailed, and that affected individual fates and the fate of a peoples in general. I did not wish to go on. All I wanted to say was that in 1991, as opposed to 1990, 1991 you had the war option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I repeat my question. Has there been any tolerance between the nationalities at that time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, from -- throughout Croatia the situation wasn't the same in areas where the Serbs were in the majority and where they were in the minority, and I'm thinking of the urban areas of Croatia when I say that. So where in parts inhabited by large numbers of Serbs they were exposed to pressure, and if they couldn't bear that pressure they had to leave their homes, which is what happened mostly during those years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, please explain us which parties dominated the elections in May 1990.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: The HDZ and the SDP. Those were the two leading parties, the two dominant parties that dominated the elections, and they won by a narrow majority, or lost. The other lost by a few places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What party was the SDP?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: The SDP was the party which inherited the League of Communists, in actual fact. And the name was the Party of Democratic Change, but before that the party was called the League of Communists. I think that's what the official title was. The League of Communists of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And the HDZ, what was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Witness, these elections took place in May 1990, and according to what you say, these elections are very significant because of the consequences. As far as the electoral campaign was concerned, was it the SDP, the former League of Communists, was it promoting the federal unity, or was -- and was HDZ campaigning for Croatia to secede from Yugoslavia? Was -- were these problems in the middle of the election or campaign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, precisely as you've just put it, Mr. President. The pre-electoral campaign of the HDZ was based on the policy of seceding from Yugoslavia, creating an independent Croatia, whereas the SDP advocated a community of states in its pre-electoral programme or electoral campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Later on there was founded the SDS. Could you please explain us what kind of party that was and when it was founded?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: The Serbian Democratic Party, well, I can't say precisely when it was established in Croatia. I assume in 1990. I can't tell you exactly. As for Podravska Slatina I know that for certain. I don't know the date, but I do know that it was the beginning of 1991. Whether it was February or March I can't quite be -- I can't be quite sure now and I don't think it's that important, but I do know that because a lot of my friends and acquaintances were involved in the whole process and so I know when the party was established there. But I can't -- and the founding Assembly was held near my workplace. So that's how I knew about it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And what kind of party was that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Well, the Serbian Democratic Party was in fact a party which, on the basis of its programme and activities, was supposed to protect the interests of the Serb people in Croatia. First of all, in its political involvement in Croatia as its founding father and president the late Dr. Raskovic used to say many a time, both in the Croatian parliament and in other public statements and appearances he made. The party programme was to be to organise the Serbian community in Croatia, thereby protecting the interests of the Serb community by asserting it in the political life through political dialogue with other participants of political life in Croatia and to protect the interests of the Serbs in Croatia. So that briefly would be the party programme if I were to paraphrase this without any pretensions of being very well acquainted with the programme, but on the basis of what I heard and saw, that's what it would have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one question. Witness, you told us that when the constitution was amended in 1990, the status of the Serbs in Croatia was also amended. They were a constituent people before, and after that they became a minority. There was this formal and official change in their status. That's one thing. But in terms of their rights, their substantial rights, in terms of their actual rights, how were -- was the status of Serbs in Croatia modified following the change in the constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps in formal terms you would not think that there were any major differences at first glance, or for me to be able to say that because I'm not well-versed in legal matters. But bringing the Serbs into a different position, from being a constituent nation to -- that is to say a people who at the beginning of the century, the 20th century, had a significant majority, and then in that same century reduced that number and expel many of them, and with their participation not only in wars but in the creation of the Croatian state in the first place as a community of nations and also through their work and cultural work help to assert the Croatian state without asking them whether they wish to be a nation or not, and when their majority status was brought into question, they weren't asked at all and they were thrown out of the constitution. So this was a symbolic pointer, indicator to how that nation would fair on a daily basis in their daily lives. That is at least how we the slightly more educated citizens thought about this, and other people felt it too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this a matter of self-determination for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One very brief follow-up question. You stated that the SDP was founded -- no. No. The Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS, was founded after the elections. It was founded by the Serbs in Croatia in order to defend the interests of the Serbs in Croatia. I want to know the following thing: Was this political party founded spontaneously and in your -- in your city, Podravska Slatina, or was this organised from Belgrade by Serb nationalists? Do you get the gist of my question? Was this, the creation of this party, something that happened spontaneously, locally, because there was a problem locally, or was this all decided and organised in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, many Serbs from Croatia went to Belgrade, but many ideas from Belgrade were not realised in Croatia. This idea that the Serbs should form, and I'm convinced of that although I can't present arguments to bear that out, but I am convinced not only because the president was Dr. Raskovic, an academician, and people around him, I'm certain that these were people who in the area where they were the ethnically dominant, and I'm thinking of the Knin, Krajina, and that part of the Krajina in general, autonomously because we're talking about intellectuals here from the urban areas and Dr. Raskovic and the group together with him, who came with him, and returned, they originated from those parts. So the Serbs in Croatia, without any suggestions from outside, they established the Serbian Democratic Party. And I'm convinced, if I can put it that way, that they sought ways and means of protecting themselves and no longer believed in the SDP and the issue of the Serbian community in Croatia in the way the Serbs voted in their masses for the SDP, and they sought a way out in the establishment of a national party, or a nationalist party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently you knew all SDP members from your town, the president, the other members. Did you yourself join this party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In 1988, I stepped down from the SDP party. I was no longer a party member until two years ago. No party, Your Honour. I was not a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the SDS was founded at the time in this town you lived in, had you heard of Mr. Seselj? Did this name ring a bell, or was it someone who was a complete unknown for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I did not see Mr. Seselj ever before except perhaps on television, but I -- well, he's a little younger than me. I know him to be an intellectual, and I think he's from the Sarajevo University or Belgrade University from there, and probably from the political section when it came to the Serbian Radical Party. So that's what I heard and knew on the basis of these sources and political information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. When the SDS was founded in the municipality of Podravska Slatina and its first president was to be Milun Karadzic, according is to you, is it possible that Mr. Seselj played a part in the creation of this party directly or indirectly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't believe so, no. Well, I don't know for certain but I don't see any logic in that either. Mr. Seselj was the president of the party in Serbia, and that party didn't exist at the time in Croatia. So my answer would be I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, you already mentioned Raskovic as one of the leaders of the SDS. Could you give us the names of the other important leaders?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: In my region, and I can tell you what I know, there was Mr. Veljko Dzakula at first, the president of the regional organisation and a close associate, fairly close associate of the late Dr. Raskovic. Then afterwards, in late 1991, I believe, there was a meeting of some kind, a rally of some kind, and from Veljko, Sasic took over, Ilija Sasic. At least that's the information I have.
