That's what I heard from those people, from Mr. Dzakula in actual fact, directly. Of course in Eastern Slavonia there was Hadzic, Jovan Opacic in Knin and some other people whose names I had heard and later on I met some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Sasic have a very important role in the party?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, in 1991 he was the president of the regional organisation of the party for our region, and I said that a moment ago. I said I had heard that from somebody I was close to, Mr. Dzakula. I heard that Ilija Sasic took this over. Now, this seemed a bit strange to me, to be quite frank, because the party did not have, if I can put it this way, such a long tradition in my region, which is the same region that Mr. Sasic comes from. But Mr. Dzakula had asserted himself more, so I thought this was a little strange but later on we were to see why that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you if Mr. Sasic also negotiated with the Croatian side once?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that in 1991 he attended negotiations with Tudjman. Well, I learnt this from the media, and people told me later on that he went to ask that certain people who had been arrested be released. I think Goran Hadzic and someone else. I can't remember their name now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You already explained us about the rising tensions in the area. Did the Serbs in your area get arms and, if so, from whom?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: In the town of Podravska Slatina, until the 30th of August while I was in town, and it's a town with 11.500 inhabitants based on the 1991 census, only Croats bore weapons around the town of Slatina. I could see that as could other citizens, and this was every day, an everyday occurrence regardless of the form it took. I did hear that the Serbs were given weapons too but, strangely enough, they didn't carry those weapons on them. But later on where I went to the areas under Serb control, I saw for myself that they did in fact have some weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was it necessary for them to get weapons?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it was necessary or not, but what I experienced is this: If you wanted to defend yourself, you had to see to that yourself, and I had to leave my own town because I feared for the lives of my family and me, so I had to leave. It was a question of life and death. And later this turned out to be the correct thing to do, because when I returned later on my friends and relatives, many of them were killed. They hadn't left. They were killed. That's the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Who organised the arming? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I'm quite certain that the weapons from the depots of the former JNA was the source. That's where the Croats and Serbs got their weapons from. Now, the weapons that the Serbs had, I'm convinced that they were from the JNA depots, from the contingent of the Territorial Defence as it was called. Now as to the Croatian side especially as concerns their institutions such as the National Guards Corps, the ZNG and the Ministry of the Interior, I don't know about that except what was seized from the barracks of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to come back to the SDS. There has been a rift inside the SDS in 1991. Can you affirm this or hasn't this been the case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. That's a leading question, and I think it's impermissible. There was a rift and then he says, "Can you confirm that?" I don't think that that is proper on the Prosecutor's part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer, it is indeed a very leading question. Can you please address the matter differently, because you're stating that there was a rift.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Sorry for that. I realised that after having put this question. I will repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Has there been a rift in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously I explained a moment ago that there were personnel changes in my region. Some of the people close to me who were in the SDS, well, I heard that the main problem in the SDS was that, if I can put it this way, the rift, when it came to the issue of whether to have an armed struggle and protection of the Serbs or to organise a pacifistic form of political involvement, if I can put it that way, seeking a solution that way. So that's where the rift occurred. And my answer is yes, there was a rift in the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of the leaders of the SDS who were for a solution by force and who were for a solution by negotiating?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am not really familiar with the structure of the SDS in the headquarters in Knin, but I am certain from what I myself heard listening to Dr. Raskovic and from what I read that he wrote and advocated in the media, he was in favour of building up and affirming the SDS and the Serbian community through political dialogue and through pointing to the problems of the Serbian community. That's how he wanted to affirm the SDS party platform. Another group, and later it transpired that the late Milan Babic had been at its head, and Milan Martic also, and in my area it was Sasic instead of Dzakula, Goran Hadzic, and so on, this was a group of people who advocated the other option, the other option being weapons, organising defence, armed resistance, protection. They spoke primarily about protection. That's how they explained it. That was where the rift in the SDS appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have the leaders been threatened, the leaders who were for a peaceful solution been threatened by the other movement?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: It wasn't just threats, Your Honour. In 1991, the president of Vrgin Most municipality, Mr. Obradovic, was killed only because he rejected that option. From what I myself know personally and from what Mr. Dzakula told me, he received threats. And not just threats, but his life was at risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Are you able to give us an example that his life was at risk?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I was present when they wanted to kill a certain group of people close to Martic. The police near the town of Novska, on the motorway, they wanted to kill Mr. Veljko Dzakula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, you told us that Ilija Sasic was following the militant movement of the SDS, that he wanted to have the problems solved by force. Do you know if he had support from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I can't really say, but I was a witness to the fact that a part of the Association of Serbs from Croatia who were in Belgrade at the time and where many of our Serbs applied for assistance because they were all people originating from our area, and previously they had held important posts, I know that this association supported the option of armed resistance and so on, but I'm sure that the legal and other forms of authority in the former Yugoslavia from the territory of Serbia did the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now addressing, I was about to say, a crucial issue as far as I'm concerned. This is extremely important. You have just said the following: You have just said that there were two groups, one group that advocated political dialogue, and the second group which wanted to resort to violent or military action, and in this second group there was Babic, Martic, and Goran Hadzic, but you add something, and this is, and this is what seems to me to be very important. You said that the second group wanted to organise the defence, resistance, in so many words, that is by the way the word which you used, or the protection of the Serbs, and that was the purpose of this group, resistance and protection and organisation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was the purpose of this second group -- now, did they have another aim, for instance? Did they have Greater Serbia in mind and the takeover of territories predominantly Croatian? This group in which Babic, Martic, and Hadzic were included, did this group also have at the back of its mind the idea of controlling a number of other territories, or according to you was the aim to organise, protect and resist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am convinced that the general goal was protection, resistance, things of that sort. But when you mention names, Your Honour, as I had an opportunity to meet those people, I have to say that they were unable to carry out more complex tasks. So it would be difficult to implement such a grand project. Now that you're asking me about the idea of a Greater Serbia, in my part of the world, I mean Western Slavonia, these are now four counties from the River Drava to the River Sava, from Slatina and Virovitica all the way to Okucani and Nova Gradiska. I never heard of the concept of a Greater Serbia except from my fellow citizens, Croats who were trying, I'm deeply convinced, to defend their own ideology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Babic, Martic, Hadzic. You met these people, didn't you? Did you know these three individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No -- well, I didn't know them well but I did meet them. I met them in the Krajina. What I want to say is that my impression of their capacities and their capabilities of carrying out a large-scale project was that they couldn't do it. I wasn't in the party, so I didn't have any opportunity of hearing about a political platform in which the term "Greater Serbia" was mentioned, but as I did meet these people, I assume if it had been included I would have heard of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Babic, Martic, and Hadzic, these men did not -- were not thinking of Greater Serbia. Their sole idea was to defend and protect themselves against the Croatians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, do you happen to know if there have been any contacts between Mr. Sasic and Seselj -- Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but it would have been very strange had there not been such contacts in view of the prevailing circumstances, his reputation and people's interest in meeting them. And later on when I had the opportunity of meeting Mr. Seselj myself, I became convinced of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I will come back to this later. Can you please explain us when the SAO Western Slavonia was created?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: The creation of the SAO Western Slavonia was in early 1991, or to be more precise, in May 1991. I'm not sure of the date. I can't recall the precise day, although there was a vote about the cultural autonomy as it was then called. But I do know the SAO Western Slavonia was already being linked to the starting of armed resistance against the possible terrorism and arrests against members of the Serbian community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Who were the main political figures in the SAO Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Well, how can I say this? I don't know who these people were, but I can tell you how I obtained my information. I asked a school friend of mine, a gentleman called Zagorac. I said, "How come you nominated the commander of Western Slavonia?" And he told me that Mr. Sasic had persuaded him to do so. He was a man who came from my town, a lawyer in a place near Daruvar where they had a meeting, and they nominated again a man from my town. So this Mr. Zagorac, I was very close to him, and I asked, "Well, how come you appointed a layman to a military post?" And he said that the SDS at its meetings organised and appointed certain military structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the SAO Western Slavonia had a representation in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Both the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the SAO Western Slavonia had their representations in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was this a kind of diplomatic mission?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't call it that. We called it the bureau of the SAO of Western Krajina. I say "we" because I was in Western Slavonia at the time, and I was one of the people responsible for certain jobs, and therefore I would visit that bureau. We thought it was a bureau that was meant to coordinate the assistance that was needed, and it was based primarily on humanitarian aid but also other forms of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You already told us that you visited this mission. Whom did you meet there when you were there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I met various people there, people from my hometown, from my hometown of Daruvar. I didn't know the other people very well. I wasn't part of those structures, and they were not members of my profession. So I had no basis on which I could know them. But I did meet both Mr. Sasic and Mr. Simpraga and a number of people who were there either as refugees, working as volunteers, or as members of that bureau that is the political part of the SDS. But as I was not a member, I don't know how come they were there, what their functions were, but I did meet various people, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Sasic the head of the mission at that time or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I think as he was the president of the Regional Board of the SDS that he was superior to the bureau. The bureau was simply an office that provided him with certain logistical support. But I don't know when Mr. Sasic stopped dealing with these matters because he only visited Western Slavonia sporadically, occasionally. I didn't have much opportunity of seeing him there. He may have come more often, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Witness, we're still talking about 1991, are we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What was your position at that time when you went there for a visit?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: The first time I went there for a visit it was December 1991. I was a refugee by then. I no longer held any post. I had just learned that people had left Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I will come to this -- back to this later. My next question: Have you ever been arrested by Croat paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before I left Slatina, that was the 29th, I think, of August, a relative of mine and I were trying to leave Slatina, and we were stopped. Many people were stopped, detained, or mistreated, but what that day -- what made that day different was we were no longer willing to stay in Slatina. We were afraid, and there I was detained and for several hours they tried to persuade me, and then they took me to the police station in Slatina, and the police released me because they knew me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: So you have been arrested or -- by these paramilitary forces outside Slatina?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Outside the town of Slatina, yes, in a village called Donji Majlani [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And they brought you to the police station later on?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Yes. They brought me to the police station, and they wanted to establish our identity, and I had resided in Slatina for more than 20 years. The police officers knew me and they had nothing against me, so they released me, but by then I was already in a state of shock and fear because of the mistreatment I had been subjected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What was your reaction after this arrest?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a combination of circumstances. When I left the police station I ran into an old friend of mine and he had a weekend cottage in a neighbouring village close to Slatina. I used to be a tenant of his and he knew me, and he saw that I was very confused and frightened. I didn't want to go home, and then he took me to his weekend cottage, that relative of mine and I to the village of Lukavac, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the gentleman's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you always remain there or did you go to another location later on?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: There we found people from neighbouring villages, mostly Serbian villages. And as this relative of mine and I were educated people, we were able to tell them what had happened. And then they asked me to go to their village and explain to the people there what the situation in Slatina was like, to tell people not to expose themselves to danger, although I have to say communications had been cut off. The roads between Podravska Slatina and the neighbouring villages had been already been cut off. This relative of mine and I went to the village of Macute, and they persuaded me to go to Vocin. They took me there, and there I met some people who were organising armed groups and setting up check-points with armed guards to separate off the villages that today make up the municipality of Vocin, but at the time there was a regional office there, and they were separating themselves off from Podravska Slatina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you move to Vocin?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Well, there was no way for me to go back from Vocin. They brought four or five us there, and I know for a fact that they asked me and my relative Milan to go to those people, because we had some education, and to explain to them what the situation was and to help them in a way. And in Vocin we ended up there as refugees. We couldn't go back, and there was no way forward either. Of course, Your Honours, I could have gone but at a great risk. My life would have been in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when was this that you moved to Vocin, which date?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: The 29th. That's when I left Slatina. I think that I went to Vocin on the 30th. I couldn't say that with certainty. Later on when I analyse the situation, I link it up with a holiday which is celebrated in the Serbian areas, the Assumption of Our Lady and it was a day or two after that. That's in October, and I think it was on the 30th that I went to Vocin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The 30th of October?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. The 30th of August, of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: When you were in Vocin have you ever been mobilised into the TO and, if so, when and where?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was mobilised but not right away. I was mobilised around the 11th or 12th, but not into the military formation. I was mobilised by the staff, and they explained to me that I would be receiving and organising accommodation for refugees, because people came from other towns and villages, just as I had done, and accommodation had to be found for them. I was not on very good terms with the people who were then in the command, and they didn't really want to have me in the ranks of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please describe us how this mobilisation took place?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I was in the house of a man called Radosevic, who is now deceased, and the relative who was there with me was mobilised right away. I was mobilised a few days later in quite a rough manner. The police came in the middle of the night. They dragged me outside, and with no explanation. I thought I was under arrest. They simply took me to the place where the command of the Territorial Defence was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Where was this? Where did they bring you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: They brought me to the Territorial Defence Staff of Podravska Slatina, was in place called Lager Sekulinci. The neighbourhood is called Omladinsko Naselje. It's a building where the scouts used to have their training over the summer. It was an improvised accommodation for a large number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I would like to show the witness 65 ter number 2868. This is a map which has already got an exhibit number, P182.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, before the map shows up on the monitor, could you describe us how were you received at this command post?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on my arrival -- well, I was actually brought there quite roughly. I raised objections with the people I knew then in the command, and I knew almost all of them. Well, maybe not all of them, but I knew quite a few of them, and of course they were quite uncomfortable with the fact that I had been treated so roughly, but from the conversations that had preceded my mobilisation and judging by the kind of people they had sent to fetch me, I couldn't have fared any better. That was the best I could hope for. The people apologised to me and they said, "Well, you know. It's wartime. You can't control everyone. You can't keep it all under control," things like that. Of course I'm convinced that this demonstrated their attitude towards me and my role and position there. That's how I understood the situation anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did they insist on your mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Well, I objected, Your Honours. I said they couldn't mobilise me in that situation -- or, rather, that no one except the formal territorial organ of the Territorial Defence, legally authorised to mobilise people for the needs of the JNA, could mobilise me because I was a reserve military officer and I was liable for military service, but they ignored everything I said. They said I should bear in mind where I was and what the circumstances were, that all formality was at an end, that we were at war, and that was the brief explanation I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you already see the map on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please show us where Lager Sekulinci is situated?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, but the part of the map I need to see is not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can the map be moved around? Or, Mr. Kulic, could you show us the direction where this Lager Sekulinci is situated?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Can we lift the map up, because it's in the southern portion. It's fine now. The red, the red circle, is Sekulinci on the left, and on the right we have another settlement where it says Gornji. And in the middle there is a small settlement with small letters. I'm afraid I can't see that either but I'm certain, because I know the area, that it's called Omladinsko Naselje, which is an area that we called Lager Sekulinci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Is it correct that it is in the south-east of Sekulinci itself?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: It's more eastward rather than south-east. It's south of the road running for -- from Sekulinci to Juricic. However, it's east of Sekulinci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. What -- when you have been mobilised, what was your first assignment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: For the first 14 days -- well, 10 to 14 days, roughly, I was wearing civilian clothes, and I was in that area of Lager Sekulinci and the surrounding parts, Vocin. I tried with the local boards as they were set up, the commands of the local boards, to organise taking in the refugees who came into the area, and those are the orders I received. It was a need, a humanitarian necessity to organise accommodation for the people pouring into the area from other regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you later get a uniform?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not quite sure when that was, when I was issued a uniform, but it was sometime in the first half of October -- or, rather, the second half of October when I was given assignments within the frameworks of the Territorial Defence command to work organising, training and education for the members of the Territorial Defence who had not done their military service previously. So this was a sort of training course that I was supposed to organise, but the question remained that it was also my duty to accommodate the incoming mobilised soldiers. Not civilians any more but soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's almost five to 6.00. We're going to have a 10-minute break. We'll resume at 5 past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We have resumed. Judge Harhoff had some business to attend to. The Prosecution has used 57 minutes. You have one hour and three minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, can you tell us when did the first volunteers arrive to Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: That was in the second half -- or, rather, the beginning of the second half of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly what the date was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know who sent these volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. The volunteers were sent by the staff, the War Staff of the Serbian Radical Party. That's what it said on the document that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please move into -- on the monitor 65 ter number 737. This is a letter to the Ministry of Serbs -- Ministry for Serbs Outside Serbia, and the Prosecution got this document from a sensitive source on the 18th of September, 2003. I guess that Dr. Seselj knows who this sensitive source is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, is this document authentic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I do believe that this document is authentic, although I haven't actually seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was this a typical letter for request of volunteers at that time? Can you say this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The question is inadmissible, Mr. President, because the witness said that he believes that the document is authentic, although he's never seen it before, and now the Prosecutor is asking him whether it's a typical letter. Now, the question that he could ask would be has he seen another letter ever?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Mr. Seselj is right. You've asked him if that is a typical letter, implying thus that he had seen other letters of this type. So you need to ask him first whether he's seen other such letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, you've heard the President's remarks. Could you answer his question?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I never saw this letter before, and I don't know this portion, but there were a -- so-called recognisable forms of correspondence, so that's why I assume that this is authentic. At the time -- at that point in time although I was in Western Slavonia myself, I did not know that volunteers were being sent. I didn't know about that. I learn that later on when I met the first volunteers. So linked to this letter I can say that I didn't know that it was being sent or whether it was being sent from people from my Territorial Defence. I see that here it says Novska, the Territorial Defence Staff Novska. I do not, however, exclude the possibility that they sent something like this from my staff. And I previously explained, Your Honours, that I wasn't close to the command in the Territorial Defence Staff where I had been -- to which I had been mobilised.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another objection, Mr. President. The Prosecutor must not lead the witness to make guesswork. All the witness can do is say what he knows personally, not to guess at the answer, whereas the Prosecutor seems to be leading him in that direction, to encourage him to guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I think the witness does not remember this document at the moment because it has been shown to him during a 92 ter statement, and he commented on this document. So it's not that I am guessing. Maybe that the witness at the moment does not remember this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you know the author of this document, Slobodan Gubic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: The gentleman you've just mentioned I did get to know and met but in a completely different context, not linked to this. I happened to meet the man when I was a member of the Banja Luka Corps. So after these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: My case manager already informed me that this witness -- this document has already been admitted into evidence. It's P239, and it is under seal. I would like to show the witness the next document, which is 65 ter number 757. It's a request from the TO Okucani.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you comment this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I don't have the complete document. I'm missing a page. All I have is the first page. And I think in English the problem is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Apparently page 2 is missing. We don't have the stamps and so on and so forth. Mr. Mussemeyer, page 2 is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. We can give it in one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, can you tell us how many volunteers arrived in the area? The document at the end of page 1 speaks about 5.000.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I can speak about the area of the Territorial Defence under the control of the Territorial Defence Staff of territorial -- of Podravska Slatina. Now, the period mentioned here up until the 13th of December, 1991, I personally think that in that area, including Zvecevo, there could not have been more than, let's say, 4 to 500 volunteers, in my own personal opinion, as far as I knew the situation and met them and so on. I don't exclude a slight deviation from that figure because I didn't have the exact figures and information as to the number and their movement. Now, with respect to the document you've just shown me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Prosecutor did not ask you about your military activities when he covered your CV. I understand that you were an officer of the JNA and that you ended your service within the JNA with the rank of lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not an officer, an army officer. I was just in the reserve composition of the Yugoslav People's Army and underwent training for reserve officers, and my rank was captain 1st class.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were captain 1st class in the reserve corps. At the time the law governing military conscription, did that law provide for volunteers to legally join the JNA or the TO, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm quite certain that the law governing the armed forces of Yugoslavia provided for just one form of organisation in such a way that the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia were organised by the Yugoslav People's Army through the Secretariat for National Defence. There was no other possibility under the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. But the army was made up of professional officers and of reservists. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The armed forces of Yugoslavia included the territorial component. That's what the law envisaged, both professional and reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To your knowledge did the law provide for a situation where reserve officers or soldiers would have joined the JNA or the TO even without having been called to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That was not provided for in any shape or form. I am convinced, although I can't speak specifically to this, that there was another important law here and that was the Law on Territorial Defence. Each republic had that and so did the federation, and they did not stipulate any forms of voluntary organisation. But the way in which things were organised followed the example, system and model of the Yugoslav People's Army, because there were what we called formations, both for units and for institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about if you were shown a document that says the exact opposite? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I would say is that I'm not sufficiently well-versed in the legal aspects of that subject, and I might have got it wrong in what I've just presented to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When these volunteers would arrive in the field, you said there were about 400 of them. To your knowledge, would they immediately join the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the first group of volunteers that I met was at the insistence of my commander. I met them personally. He wanted to boast about that. So from the documents that the volunteers brought with them and what my commander was supposed to do, those volunteers had in fact come in to be subordinated and become attached to the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Podravska Slatina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You heard that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I saw it on the documents those volunteers brought with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a belated objection. You asked a number of questions, so it took me a little time to get my objection in, but let me remind you that the Prosecutor's question was how many volunteers were there in Western Slavonia, indicating that this document mentions a figure of 5.000, thereby trying to mislead the witness. The witness said that there were 4 or 500 to the best of his knowledge. However, we should look at the document and see that this was the need for volunteers, and the document is dated the 2nd of December. So what the Territorial Defence in Okucani assesses that they need, which is 5.000 volunteers. And I think it's quite out of order for the Prosecution to pose questions based on falsification of what it actually says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Mussemeyer, I also understand that this figure of 5.000 was an estimate of a number of men needed. It's not the figure of -- of the men who actually arrived. The witness told us that there were about 400 to 500 of them. Witness, would you agree that this figure of 5.000 is an assessment of the needs, but there weren't 5.000 volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just read this document and I can see that it is an assessment, an estimation, but it refers to a far larger territory than the one I spoke about. So I spoke about the area under the control of the Territorial Defence Staff of Podravska Slatina, which is where I was. So I can give you an estimate for that judging by the number of people I met and the information I got and so on. But when we're dealing with SAO Western Slavonia, then you must bear in mind, Your Honours, that there were four more Territorial Defence Staffs there in the municipalities up to the River Sava, and the Territorial Defence Staff of Novska, this one in the village of Rajic which is along the main road, it's close to the Sava River. So these were assessments for the whole of Western Slavonia. At least that's how I understand it reading this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document mention is made of an axis Virovitica, your own municipality, Daruvar, Pakrac, Okucani, Banja Luka, and to the east there is the Belgrade-Zagreb axis, and so on and so forth. Would that figure of 5.000 include all these axes, or is that a figure that is only relevant to the Okucani municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. From this context, as far as I understand it, and I think it corresponds to the situation, that this was for the entire area of SAO Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. To the entire area. Thus five thousand volunteers are needed for the entire region. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Is it my turn now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I also had doubts about this 5.000, and it was exactly the reason I was asking the witness to clarify this. The reason was not to mislead. Can I have this document moved into evidence. I understood that we already got the second page in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't received the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: It is in the e-mail, I was told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but Mr. Seselj has not received it. I'm talking about the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received it on paper, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Any objections, Mr. Seselj, to the admission of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But once again, the question is what does this document have to do with this witness if the witness says he's never seen it before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's another matter altogether. Can we have a number, Registrar, please for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P264.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have on the monitor the document 65 ter number 582. This is an already admitted exhibit. It has the number P227 and is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you see this document on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can't see the upper part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: This is a letter from Mr. Zoran Rankic, who was the deputy of the War Staff of the SRS. Please, Mr. Seselj, correct me if I'm saying this wrong. And it was written the 16th of October, 1991. There are mentioned in this letter three conditions under which the SRS would send volunteers to Western Slavonia. Mr. Witness, can you see this?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if these conditions have been fulfilled?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. First of all, the Prosecutor should ask the witness whether he's ever seen this document before, and if he says yes, then he can go on and ask him whether these conditions were met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Mussemeyer, that's what I was about to say. This document is sent to the Territorial Defence of his municipality. You need to ask him whether he was aware of this document at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you tell us if this document is authentic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I assume it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not the proper question to ask. You asked him if the document is authentic. You should ask him first whether he's seen the document before. Then yes, he may say the document is authentic because there is a stamp or, no, here a signature. I'll ask the question myself. Witness, we have a document dated 16th of October, 1991. At the time, did you see that document? Did you read that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Why, then, would this document be authentic according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For a number of reasons. It was not difficult to assume, and I knew the way in which communication was maintained between organs and institutions, but I say that I assume that it's authentic, and later on I came across certain documents from this same institution. That's why I say I assume that it is, but I cannot claim that it is because I've never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness is brought into a situation where he's asked to speculate again. I did not challenge the authenticity of this document, but it's inappropriate for this witness to be asked whether it's an authentic document or not. How can he say whether it is or not? All he can do is speculate, and there should be no speculation in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, you assume that this document is authentic. You added that you saw other documents coming from the same organisations. So I understand that you had the opportunity to read documents from the SRS. Am I right? Did I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a moment ago when I was asked whether I know when the first volunteers arrived into the area of Vocin, I said when and how they arrived, and on that occasion I was able to see documents. Now, later on, if this is a topic discussed by this Tribunal, I can say that I met some people too. So I knew something about these lines of communication. That's why I say I assume that it is, but I can't claim that it is because it's a document I've never seen before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, based on the substance and the contents of this document, and based on other information you had, based on what you saw, you are in a position to conclude that this document may be an authentic document, that it is a document addressed by the SRS to the Territorial Defence of Podravska Slatina. Is that what you were telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness 65 ter number 594, which has already been admitted into evidence under P228, and it is under seal. It's an answering letter from the 19th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you see this document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if it is authentic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's an authentic document, although I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an authentic document because of its content or because of what has been added to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for both reasons and because of the signature of the person I know it's authentic. I recognise the shape and manner of handwriting and also the form of the letter. I have been educated to recognise these things, so I feel I'm competent to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how was the approach of the JNA officers in your region? Did they agree to the arrival of the volunteers to support the Serbs in the area?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: In the area I was in there were no active-duty JNA officers except for the commander of the Territorial Defence Staff of Western Slavonia who arrived in November, Colonel Jovan Trbojevic. There were no other active-duty officers unless they came sporadically. I pointed this out to my colleagues and superiors as an omission. I know for a fact that opinions were divided in the Territorial Defence regarding the arrival of volunteers. Not so much their arrival as the special status they had and their behaviour, their conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I will come to this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can I please have the document 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a little bit lost. There's something I don't understand. Why do you need to show this document which has already been admitted, and we could gain some time by putting the questions directly, couldn't we, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The witness is a witness of the area. He knows what happened there, and I want to lead him through -- also through the documents. If you think it's not necessary, I can also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents which have already been admitted, well, there's no need in showing them again unless, of course, they are of any particular interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Yes. The next one has already been admitted, but I want to show it, nevertheless, to the witness because I think it's quite important. It's 65 ter number 608, which has been admitted as P223 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: This is a letter from -- to the Territorial Defence of Podravska Slatina, an authorisation, and it authorises Mr. Radovan Novacic to be the commander of the volunteers in the area, and I would like to know from the witness who was the commander of the volunteers. Was it Mr. Novacic or was it a JNA commander?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I met Radovan Novacic when the first group of volunteers arrived. A letter was sent by the staff of the Radical Party regarding the 17 volunteers, and Mr. Radovan Novacic was the only one whose first and last name was mentioned. I remember that because I met the man, and I asked for other details because of the security issue. I didn't even know who Radovan Novacic was, and I said to the commander, he could be anyone. That's why I went to meet Mr. Novacic, and later on I would meet him. The volunteer units had their own command, and the staff of the Territorial Defence of Western Slavonia was in charge of them. But I'm sure that with respect to the first group it was the Podravska Slatina Territorial Defence Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was there a kind of double line in command?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I was a reserve officer so I knew a little bit about how command goes on, and I felt that the biggest problem was that there was not a unified form of command, that these were separate units and there was a separate type of linked command. The territorial staff of Western Slavonia was in command of volunteers on the territory of the Podravska Slatina Territorial Defence Staff. That's the information I received from my colleagues in the Territorial Defence Staff where I myself had certain duties to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if the volunteers -- did they abide to the rules of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. The Prosecutor is going too fast. Once again here we are addressing a crucial issue, and it's important that we spend some time on it. You are at the headquarters of the Territorial Defence. You see volunteers coming in. Now, there's a document which we have before us which mentions Radovan Novacic. What I would like to know is this: When this man and the other people arrive, is he put under the command of the Main Staff of the Territorial Defence of Podravska Slatina? That's my question. This is a very precise question. Is he going to obey the orders of the Main Staff of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was in October, and this was the first group of volunteers. There was 17 of them, and they were under the command of the Territorial Defence Staff of Podravska Slatina. We are not now talking about other groups and other times. I'm speaking only of the first group and how I met the person mentioned in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, he arrived in October. At what time did he get there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think they arrived in the second half of October, but I couldn't pinpoint the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are 17 all in all; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And these 17 men are commanded by Radovan Novacic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just said that they are put under the command of the TO Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. That's what I said, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what is the name of the commander of the TO in Podravska Slatina? Who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Boro Radosavljevic. And the commander of the army, so to say, the Territorial Defence Staff, it also replaced the civilian authorities. That's why I'm trying to explain all this to you. And the commander of the military who received -- I'm referring to the military territorial component, was a friend of mine, Captain 1st Class Keleuva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I've understood you well, Boro Radosavljevic. I'm sorry if I have misspelled [as interpreted] your names -- so this person Boro Radosavljevic is a commander. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Territorial Defence of Podravska Slatina municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Radovan Novacic will then obey his orders; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whose orders he obeyed because I was not in the chain of command, but I know that he came. He brought a letter that his unit, that first unit, was to be part of the Territorial Defence Staff. It was to be one of their units. And the officers from the staff informed me of this fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in the Main Staff if Radovan Novacic is told, "Go there, do this and that," will Radovan Novacic obey the orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. According to the system of subordination he had to, and he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. And that's what he did. Prosecutor, you have the floor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, could you tell us who was Colonel Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Colonel Jovan Trbojevic was an active duty officer of the Yugoslav People's Army, and he originated from that area. He arrived, I think, in early November, or sometime in November to the post of Staff Commander of the Territorial Defence of Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could I please have 65 ter number 501 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, could you comment on this document? It's the assignment or the appointment of Jovan Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it follows from this document that Colonel Trbojevic was deployed to this job on the 20th of September, but he arrived probably two months later on, not much less than that if not that. Evidently this is an order where the personnel administration of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence in the usual way assigned people to their duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can I have admitted this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P265.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, can you tell us if Mr. Trbojevic had command over the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: In the Territorial Defence Staff of Podravska Slatina as of the 1st of November my colleagues, the officers and the Staff Commander, assured me of that. They said that the volunteers from Serbia would be under the command of Colonel Trbojevic. I'm not absolutely certain, but I think that at a meeting of officers I heard that from Trbojevic himself also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you describe us what was the volunteers' behaviour in the area of Vocin?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all I have to say something, namely that the meagre knowledge I have of military skills and organisation is to say that for an army to be an army it has to have a unified system of command and they have to wear uniforms or dress the same and so on and so forth, and this was not the case. The volunteers had a certain amount of autonomy. They organised their own accommodation and also their own command so that in relation to the members of the Territorial Defence Staff, they were differently dressed, and they conducted themselves differently. I couldn't say right now that they walked around with weapons and the others didn't, they all did. The difference was in that the members of the volunteer units, some of them, of course, I can't say that about all of them, but some of them went from house to house and they behaved towards the hosts, the local families, in such a way that people were afraid of them. I heard that from four or five families. They demanded to be given brandy, coffee, food. And when some people had already been killed, the local people were afraid of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What was the reputation of the volunteers among the local people?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Well, their reputation was -- how can I put it? The local people didn't like the volunteers to come into their courtyards. They didn't even like that, but the volunteers didn't care. They didn't think about that. In November, the overall situation on the ground in the area of Vocin and the surrounding area was such that people were very frightened. And then they were even more frightened when strange people arrived, unknown people, and all kinds of rumours went around, and these people communicated in a manner that frightened people, so people were afraid of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Seselj arrived in the Vocin area sometime in this time period?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that was the only time I had occasion to see Mr. Seselj. I happened to be in the command in the building in Vocin when, escorted by politicians and members of the staff of Western Slavonia and Slatina, Mr. Seselj and his companions arrived, greeted everyone present including me. And from the information available to the public, I knew who he was. I think this was sometime in the second half of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When he arrived, was he wearing civilian clothes or military clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't answer with precision. He might have been in military uniform or in civilian clothing. I really can't say right now, because it didn't seem significant to me at the time. The charisma of Mr. Seselj, his fame overshadowed these details. I had the opportunity to see him wearing a uniform in the media, but I don't know if he was wearing a uniform on that occasion. I assume he was, but I can't say for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who accompanied Dr. Seselj at that time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I'm certain about some of them. Our commander of the Territorial Defence of Vocin, Mr. Rajko Bojcic as the host. Mr. Veljko Vukelic. I'm sure of that. I think there was also Mr. Sasic, but I'm not sure of that. There was quite large group of people. I knew quite a few of them from Slatina. There were also others I didn't know, so I can't be sure. But I'm sure Mr. Boro Radosavljevic was there as the commander of the overall territorial staff of Podravska Slatina. And I couldn't enumerate them all. I may be wrong if I mention more names because I wouldn't be sure if they were really there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Has there been any event with the house of the Matanci family, and if so, can you please describe this to us?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Matanci family house was torched. I was almost a witness to this. And of course this frightened me. It upset me. It made me angry, because I was an officer of sorts in a place where the headquarters, the command was, and a house had been torched. At the time I was passing by the house, and on approaching the house along the footpath I ran into three volunteers. I passed by the house. Something seemed odd, but I ignored it, and I passed by together with my companions. I was going to visit some friends of mine, the Debrojevic family. About half an hour later or three-quarters of an hour later, it was getting dark, on my way back I saw the house on fire. So I said to my companions, "Look here. It must have been those three volunteers who set fire to the house." But that's just an assumption of mine. I don't want to hurt anyone. I thought it was strange that there was a light in all three windows facing the road and there was no electric power in Vocin at the time, and people had only petroleum lamps and there weren't many of those because people didn't normally keep those in the house because they all had electricity. So how come the light was there? And of course the fire had been kindled deliberately. I wanted us to organise and go and put the fire out, but people tried to evade this. They avoided it. They were afraid. The firefighters didn't come. I assume it was those three lads I had seen before and who were members of the volunteer unit. I assume it was them who set fire to the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The Matanci family, what ethnicity were they of?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: The Matanci family were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to them later?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: I heard later on, because some very good friends of mine live nearby, and I still go to visit them and I have some land there, that family, well, they were really two elderly people, a husband and wife. They were -- Matanci. They were killed on the 13th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Kulic, can you tell us if there has been the disappearance of people in Vocin in the beginning of December?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN KULIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first time I was granted permission to leave Vocin and the area by Colonel Trbojevic on the 8th of December, and then I got ready to go, and I did go in the morning of the 9th to Banja Luka, but in the evening of the 8th of December I went to see some friends of mine who wanted me to take some things of theirs to Banja Luka because their children and wives had been evacuated previously. I mean young children under the age of seven. And I went to see them to see to ask if they still wanted me to take those things and when I should take them, and I found a group of women in the centre of Vocin in front of the health clinic and they were crying and I asked the women why they were crying and they said our children are missing. I didn't know what this was about because I wasn't from there so I didn't know them, so I said what do you mean your children are missing? It turned out that these were four young men who throughout that autumn had been engaged in the warehouse working on preparing food, wood, firewood, fuel, loading, unloading, and this was organised by the command of the village of Vocin. And these four lads had not turned up, and there were some four or five women there, and I took them to the command of the Territorial Defence, to the -- in front of the building. I asked Commander Bojcic to explain to those women where their children were. The commander didn't explain that but started talking about his parents and so on, and I thought this was irresponsible. So I said to him in front of those women, "The commander's name is Rajko Bojcic, and if he does not establish where your children are in -- within 24 hours, I myself will ask that he be held responsible with the prosecutor." And I did that later on. I learned that those children were missing from information I had received from the local people in Vocin when I met them later after they had withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are telling us many things, and it's all mixed up. Let me go back to the Matanci family house that was torched by three individuals. You were an officer at the Main Staff. Did you tell the commander that three individuals who were under his command had torched this house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told the commander, Your Honours, that I had seen three persons and that I asked for an investigation to be carried out and to establish who was responsible for the torching of that house, and I expressed my suspicions that it had been done by three lads belonging to the Volunteer Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You did your job. What did the commander do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think he ignored it. I think he was busy, but he didn't take any action regarding this request that his men investigate this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why? Why, because he was incompetent or because he was covering that type of behaviour, hiding it, or because he thought that it was just a minor incident? Why did nothing happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, Your Honour, I think that this gentleman was not up to the job. I think he was not competent to carry out those duties. I mentioned a little while ago that the territorial staff of Western Slavonia was in charge of those units. That was the staff at Zvecevo. That's where there was a Territorial Defence Staff. But in spite of this, I think one can say that my commander did not attach great significance to that event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll proceed tomorrow because it's 7.00 p.m. I'm going to ask the registrar to check the time, because at 10 to 7.00 he told me that the Prosecution had used up one hour and 15 minutes. It seems rather surprising to me, because at 18.05 I had said that the Prosecution had one hour and three minutes left. So over 45 minutes the Prosecutor would have used only 15 minutes? I would be surprised to learn that I'd been the only one to speak during all this time. I'm being told that the Prosecutor has used one hour and 23 minutes in total. I am a bit taken aback, but that's the way it is. Tomorrow the Prosecutor will have 37 minutes left. Here we have to do a lot of maths all the time. Thirty-seven minutes for the Prosecution tomorrow at 2.45. We may not be able to complete the testimony of the witness because Mr. Seselj has two hours to cross-examine the witness, so we'll probably not complete the testimony, but you never know what may happen. At any rate, the other witness needs to be ready to start testifying. I'll see you tomorrow at 2.45. Until tomorrow, Witness, you're not to have any contact with the Prosecution. You've taken the solemn declaration. You're a witness of the Tribunal. No contacts with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 5th day of March, 2008, at 2.45 p.m. 23 24
